title: Harnessing Bayesian Statistics to Accelerate Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation
abstract_summary: The paper develops a unified statistical framework for quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) and introduces Bayesian Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (BIQAE), which injects Bayesian inference into IQAE to improve measurement efficiency. Analytic proofs and numerical experiments show BIQAE yields rigorous interval estimates, achieves a consistent double-digit percentage reduction in quantum sample complexity compared with IQAE and other methods, and delivers practical gains for estimating amplitudes and molecular ground-state energies.
methodology_description: The authors develop a unified statistical framework for quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) and introduce Bayesian Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (BIQAE), which injects Bayesian inference into Iterative QAE (IQAE). They formalize amplified estimation, construct hybrid (K,N)-schedules (base-3 and base-3/base-5) to track quadrant/phase ambiguities, and derive asymptotic mean-squared-error (AMSE) and sample-complexity bounds under normal approximations. Two concrete BIQAE implementations are given: Normal-BIQAE (conjugate normal prior, delta-method approximation for prior propagation, normal-approximate likelihood) and Beta-BIQAE (conjugate beta prior, exact binomial likelihood, sampling-based beta prior fitting via MLE at stage transitions). The algorithmic pipeline per stage comprises (i) BayesianUpdate of the posterior from prior + Binomial sampling outcomes, (ii) ComputeCRI to obtain credible intervals for the amplified probability and map to an interval for the angle θ, (iii) a linear-search-based FindNextK that chooses the next amplification factor K (Kt = 2kt+1) consistent with interval containment, and (iv) PreparePrior that transforms the posterior to a prior for the next stage via the nonlinear mapping pkt+1 = sin^2(Kt+1 · f_t(pkt)). The authors analyze sample-complexity reductions attributable to the Bayesian updates, prove theoretical complexity bounds, and validate numerically via two classes of experiments: (A) synthetic amplitude estimation scaling studies (mock Grover/Q operators implemented as RY gates to emulate Q^k for classical simulation) across target accuracies and amplitudes, comparing BIQAE variants to IQAE (Chernoff-Hoeffding and Clopper–Pearson variants), BAE, MLQAE, FQAE, QAES and Classical QAE; (B) molecular ground-state energy estimation (H2, LiH, HF, BeH2) where electronic Hamiltonians are generated with PySCF and Qiskit Nature (frozen core, Jordan–Wigner mapping, qubit tapering), ground states prepared by VQE (Efficient SU(2) ansatz, SLSQP optimizer), and expectation values of Pauli terms estimated with BIQAE and compared to IQAE-CP and Classical QAE. Performance metrics include quantum sample complexity (oracle calls / weighted shots), credible interval radii, coverage rates, median absolute error, and percent improvements. Repetitions and statistical summaries are used (e.g., 200–1000 independent runs) to produce robust comparisons.
algorithms_used: Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) for state preparation
experimental_setup: Classical numerical experiments. For amplitude-scaling studies the authors used a mock Q operator (single RY(2kθ) gate) to emulate Q^k to permit large-scale classical simulation; experiments varied target accuracies across many orders of magnitude, used incremental shot batch size Nincre = 10, and repeated runs (e.g., 200 or 1000 repetitions) to compute statistics. For molecular energy estimation: electronic Hamiltonians generated at Hartree–Fock level via PySCF and Qiskit Nature with frozen core orbitals, Jordan–Wigner mapping and qubit tapering; ground states prepared via VQE using an Efficient SU(2) ansatz with full entanglement, classical SLSQP optimizer, number of layers and max iterations per molecule as listed (see experiment_parameters). Expectation values for Pauli terms were computed classically via Qiskit Runtime Estimator (zero shots) and then fed into QAE subsystems. No physical QPU was used.

amplitude_tests.inputs: Synthetic single-parameter quantum states with specified amplitude a; representative worst-case amplitude a=0.5 used for scaling studies
amplitude_tests.sizes: Varied by target accuracy; per-stage shot batches sized by Nincre (10) and adaptive Nt per stage (often small, Nt < 100)
amplitude_tests.preprocessing: Mock Q operator construction (RY gate emulation) so classical simulation has access to true θ but algorithm treats it as unknown

molecular_tests.Hamiltonian_generation: PySCF (Hartree–Fock) via Qiskit Nature; frozen core; Jordan–Wigner mapping; qubit tapering
molecular_tests.state_preparation: VQE with Efficient SU(2) ansatz; parameters optimized by SLSQP
molecular_tests.preprocessing: Pauli-term decomposition, ordering of Pauli strings by expectation magnitude; classical preparation of expectation values via Qiskit Runtime Estimator (0 shots) before QAE

experiment_process.overview: Iterative stage-based amplified estimation with Bayesian updates
detailed_steps: Initialize: choose initial k0 = 0 (K0 = 1), set prior for pkt (either normal: N(µ0,Δ2) or beta: Beta(a0,b0)), set overall confidence α (default 0.05) and schedule parameters (base-3 or base-3/base-5).
- Build circuit with kt Grover-like amplifications (mocked as RY(2kθ) in amplitude experiments or actual Qk construction in conceptual accounting).
- Sample Nk outcomes (incrementing in batches of Nincre=10 per iteration) and compute empirical mean ¯Xt (Binomial likelihood).

- BayesianUpdate: update posterior of pkt via conjugacy: for Normal-BIQAE use normal approximation to Binomial (CLT) and closed-form posterior; for Beta-BIQAE use Beta posterior (apost = a0 + Nt ¯Xt, bpost = b0 + Nt(1−¯Xt)).
- ComputeCRI: obtain credible interval for pkt (quantiles of posterior) and map to θ interval via fk mapping (arcsin/arccos with known quadrant lt).

- Determine next amplification knext by linear search ensuring the θ credible interval is contained in one of the reference intervals for the candidate K; if knext > kt then PreparePrior for next stage.

- PreparePrior: transform posterior to prior for pkt+1 via pkt+1 = sin^2(Kt+1 · ft(pkt)). For Normal-BIQAE use delta-method approximation to get new normal prior mean/variance; for Beta-BIQAE sample R=1000 draws from posterior, apply transform, and fit MLE beta parameters (a0,t+1,b0,t+1).
- Stop when interval radius for a is ≤ target ε.

Molecular pipeline: prepare Hamiltonian, run VQE to get approximate ground-state statevector (classical expectation values), then for each Pauli term use QAE subroutines above to estimate expectation values with BIQAE or comparator methods (IQAE-CP, Classical QAE). Aggregate Pauli-term estimates to form energy and compare to exact diagonalization.
experiment_process.hyperparameters_and_control: Incremental shot batch size Nincre = 10, R (beta prior fit sample) = 1000, confidence α = 0.05 with αt = α/T per stage, minimum per-stage shots (enforced for Normal methods) typically ≥ 30 to avoid zero variance pathology, K-schedules: base-3 Kt = 3^t or base-3/base-5 hybrid.

metrics: Quantum sample complexity (Noracle) — counted as weighted shots (either k or K = 2k+1 depending on convention)
Median absolute error of amplitude estimates
Credible interval radii for a and θ
Coverage rates (proportion of repetitions where true parameter lies in interval)
Percent reduction in sample complexity vs baselines
Molecular ground-state energy interval centers and radii (Hartree) and deviations from exact diagonalization
experiment_output.output_format: Tabulated numerical comparisons across target accuracies and amplitudes; empirical curves (Noracle vs ε), statistics aggregated over repetitions (means, medians, percentiles), and plots of energy vs bond length with intervals

experiment_parameters.target_accuracies_tested: varied across orders of magnitude; examples ε in {1e-2..1e-8}

repetitions.amplitude_scaling: 1000 for many studies; 200 in some comparisons

experiment_parameters.molecular_ansatz: Efficient SU(2) ansatz with full entanglement

hardware_details.simulation_environment: Classical numerical simulation; mock Q operator (RY(2kθ)) used to emulate Grover iterations for amplitude-scaling experiments
software_used: Qiskit Runtime Estimator primitive (used with zero shots to compute expectation values classically)
hardware_details.quantum_hardware: No QPU used; all experiments run via classical simulation / classical VQE expectation evaluation

reproducibility_notes.code_availability: Authors provide code on GitHub: http://www.github.com/Kirin0570/BIQAE and reference BAE companion code (alexandra-frca/BAE) with minor modifications
reproducibility_notes.data_and_parameters: Pseudocode, algorithm modules (BayesianUpdate, ComputeCRI, PreparePrior) and parameter choices (Nincre, R, alpha) are described in detail in the manuscript and appendices; VQE and Hamiltonian generation settings (mapping, frozen core, tapering) are specified
reproducibility_notes.notes: Molecular Hamiltonians are reproducible via PySCF + Qiskit Nature; random-seed and repetition counts are provided in text. Normal-BIQAE relies on normal approximations (requires moderate per-stage sample sizes); Beta-BIQAE uses a sampling-based beta-fit that is computationally cheap at stage transitions.

key_findings: [supported] The paper introduces Bayesian Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (BIQAE), a Bayesian variant of Iterative QAE (IQAE) that injects Bayesian inference into the iterative schedule.

[supported] BIQAE (both Normal- and Beta-implementations) is proven analytically to reduce quantum sample complexity relative to IQAE under the stated model assumptions; mathematical bounds and proofs are provided.

[supported] Numerical simulations (classical emulation) show Beta-BIQAE outperforms IQAE (Clopper–Pearson variant), BAE, Classical QAE, MLQAE, FQAE, QAES and canonical QAE in quantum sample complexity for estimation of an amplitude a=0.5 across many target accuracies.

[supported] The authors attribute the measured improvement in sample complexity specifically to the use of Bayesian inference (posterior/credible-interval information) rather than to other algorithmic changes; they provide both analytic derivations and numerical comparisons to support this claim.

[supported] Regression of log(sample complexity) vs log(error) indicates Beta-BIQAE scales as Noracle ∝ ε^{-1.0088} (quadratic improvement over classical sampling) while Classical QAE scales as Noracle ∝ ε^{-1.9821}.

[supported] Beta-BIQAE consistently reduces quantum sample complexity relative to IQAE-CP by roughly a near-constant factor (~12–16% depending on settings) across a wide range of amplitudes and target accuracies.

[supported] For molecular ground-state energy estimation (H2, LiH, HF, BeH2) estimated from VQE-prepared states, Beta-BIQAE achieves substantially smaller interval radii than Classical QAE at equal quantum sample complexity (e.g., median interval radius reductions reported: HF ×32.84, H2 ×14.2, BeH2 ×12.16, LiH ×12.13).

[supported] For the molecular tests, Beta-BIQAE often reduces total quantum sample complexity by orders of magnitude relative to Classical QAE to reach the same target energy accuracy (authors report 2–3 orders of magnitude for ε=10^-3 in many cases), and a persistent ~8–13% improvement over IQAE-CP.

[supported] Normal-BIQAE admits closed-form conjugate updates and analytic bounds (using normal approximations and delta method), while Beta-BIQAE (with conjugate beta prior) is preferred in small-shot regimes; the paper documents both approaches and their domains of applicability.

[speculative] The authors propose that Bayesian optimization or Bayesian-informed K,N scheduling could further improve BIQAE constants and performance; this is suggested as future work and not demonstrated.

[speculative] The paper discusses possible extension and noise-aware modifications for near-term (NISQ) hardware but notes tradeoffs (noise vs depth) and leaves practical noise-aware BIQAE schedules as an open problem.

[supported] IQAE (with Chernoff–Hoeffding or Clopper–Pearson intervals) is derived within the BIQAE framework as the limiting case of BIQAE with noninformative priors; thus IQAE can be viewed as a Bayesian method with flat/uninformative priors in this framing.

[speculative] The authors suggest BIQAE could be combined with other measurement-cost reduction techniques (and used for excited states / tomography) to expand its impact—these applications are proposed but not experimentally validated here.

[supported] All theoretical results are accompanied by mathematical proofs in the paper's appendices and by numerical experiments (code made available) supporting the claims within the idealized/noiseless simulation setting used.
results_summary: This preprint introduces Bayesian Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (BIQAE), a Bayesian augmentation of IQAE, and demonstrates via analytic proofs and classical numerical simulations that BIQAE reduces quantum sample complexity relative to IQAE and other contemporary QAE variants. Two implementations are developed—Normal-BIQAE (analytically tractable via conjugate normal approximations) and Beta-BIQAE (better for small-shot regimes). Across benchmark amplitude estimation tasks and molecular ground-state energy estimation (VQE-prepared states for H2, LiH, HF, BeH2), Beta-BIQAE consistently lowers measurement cost (sample complexity) and interval radii, commonly achieving a near-constant ~12–16% reduction versus IQAE-CP and far larger reductions versus Classical QAE, with theoretical bounds and regression evidence supporting quadratic scaling improvements.
performance_claims: Beta-BIQAE sample-complexity scaling: slope −1.0088, intercept 0.0211 (log-log regression fit R^2 = 0.9999).
Classical QAE sample-complexity scaling: slope −1.9821, intercept −1.1693 (log-log regression fit R^2 = 0.9996).
Beta-BIQAE reduces measurement cost relative to IQAE-CP by ~12–16% across many amplitudes and target accuracies (examples: ~14% improvement reported over six orders of magnitude in ε).
In molecular ground-state energy estimation, interval radii reductions of Beta-BIQAE vs Classical QAE: HF ×32.84, H2 ×14.2, BeH2 ×12.16, LiH ×12.13 (averages reported over repetitions).

For molecular energy estimation to ε=10^-3, Beta-BIQAE requires 2–3 orders of magnitude fewer samples than Classical QAE (reported across bond lengths and molecules); for HF at ε=10^-4 a three order magnitude reduction is reported.

Normal-BIQAE per-stage sample complexity upper bound: Noracle,t ≤ (z_{α_t/2}^2 / (4 K_t)) (1/ε_t^2 − 1/ε_{t−1}^2), indicating reduction proportional to previous-stage interval radius (analytic bound).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper provides analytic proofs (AMSE/sample-complexity bounds) and classical numerical simulations showing a consistent, reproducible reduction in quantum sample complexity for BIQAE (especially Beta-BIQAE) relative to IQAE, BAE, and Classical QAE in the noiseless/idealized simulation setting; thus the advantage is demonstrated in theory and in numerical experiments under the authors' assumptions and models. Practical realization on noisy hardware is acknowledged as unaddressed and speculative.
limitations: Performance and theoretical guarantees for Normal-BIQAE rely on normal approximations and the delta method; these approximations require sufficiently large per-stage sample sizes Nt and may break down in the small-sample regime.

Beta-BIQAE uses a beta-family approximation for the transformed prior (PreparePrior sampling + MLE). The method assumes the beta family can closely approximate the true transformed prior, but no general mathematical guarantee is provided that this holds in every case.

Analytic quantum-sample-complexity upper bounds are derived for Normal-BIQAE (and for hybrid-scheduled IQAE variants) but no comparable closed-form theoretical complexity bound is provided for Beta-BIQAE; numerical evidence is used instead.

Simulations of amplitude-estimation scaling used a simplified/mocked Q-operator (RY(2kθ)) to emulate Grover amplification. While circuit depths and oracle call counts were reported, the classical experiments do not model realistic gate errors, decoherence, or noise present on actual quantum hardware.

Molecular ground-state results used VQE-prepared states computed in classical simulation with zero-shot estimator calls (Estimator primitive with zero shots), i.e., state preparation and measurement noise were not modeled in the end-to-end quantum experiment.

The algorithmic schedules and proofs rely on assumptions (e.g., Assumption 1 small-angle for AAE, Assumption 2 for base-3 hybrid schedule) and asymptotic normal approximations. Practical violations of these assumptions (e.g., amplified angles near reference-interval boundaries) require fallback strategies and affect constants in bounds.

There is a practical tradeoff between applying many Grover operators (to gain statistical efficiency) and noise-induced bias in near-term devices (decay of probabilities toward 1/2). The paper acknowledges this tradeoff but does not provide a general solution that fully resolves it for NISQ hardware.

Normal-BIQAE and other normal-based methods exhibit degraded coverage and performance at small per-stage sample sizes compared to beta-based methods; a minimum-shot workaround was used (e.g., min 30 shots) but this increases practical cost.

Beta-BIQAE requires sampling (R samples) and an MLE fit at each stage transition to prepare priors. Although authors claim the classical cost is small in practice (T=O(log(1/ε)) times and R maybe ~1000), this classical sampling + fitting step is an added complexity and could become non-negligible for different parameter regimes or very tight latency requirements.

[inferred] The numerical comparisons and reported constant-factor improvements are obtained in idealized/noiseless simulation conditions; the same improvements may shrink or vanish under realistic hardware noise or correlated error models.

[inferred] The molecular study covered only a few small molecules (H2, LiH, HF, BeH2) with specific mappings and tapering; scalability and performance for larger, chemically relevant systems remain untested.
[inferred] Some proofs and bounds are asymptotic (AMSE and normal approximation); finite-sample, non-asymptotic guarantees for BIQAE (especially Beta-BIQAE) are limited or absent.

[inferred] The base-3 and base-3/base-5 hybrid schedule analyses depend on moderate assumptions about the confidence-interval radii across stages (Assumption 2 or related lower bounds); in pathological instances these conditions might fail and constant factors could worsen.
open_questions: How to optimally inject Bayesian inference at the level of hyperparameters and (K, N)-scheduling decisions (beyond interval/posterior updates) to further reduce measurement cost?

Can Bayesian optimization methods reliably and efficiently tune BIQAE hyperparameters (e.g., per-stage Nt, incremental batch size Nincre, schedule choices) to improve the constant prefactor of the quantum-sample-complexity in practice?

What are the best noise-aware scheduling strategies (limits on number of Grover operators, modified bases, or alternative amplification strategies) to balance noise-induced bias and statistical efficiency on current NISQ hardware?

How robust are BIQAE's advantages (both Normal- and Beta-based implementations) under realistic noise models (e.g., amplitude damping, depolarizing noise, readout errors, gate-dependent errors) and device-specific error correlations?

Does the beta-family prior approximation remain sufficiently accurate for the prior transformation in all practical regimes? Under what circumstances would the beta family fail to approximate the true transformed prior well, and what broader families or nonparametric approaches would be preferable?
What are the finite-sample (non-asymptotic) performance guarantees for Beta-BIQAE, including coverage properties and exact sample-complexity bounds?
How to best combine BIQAE with error mitigation or error-correcting strategies to retain the Bayesian advantage when noise is significant?
How does BIQAE scale with system size in practical quantum chemistry problems (larger molecules, more qubits, more Pauli terms)? Do the constant-factor improvements persist as problem size increases?

How well does BIQAE perform for other amplitude-estimation applications beyond expectation-value and ground-state energy estimation — e.g., derivative estimates, probabilistic outputs in quantum machine learning, or option pricing in finance?
Can BIQAE be adapted to efficiently identify excited states (the authors mention combining with tomography) and how does Bayesian scheduling interact with tomography requirements?

What modifications are required to implement BIQAE on current hardware (superconducting, trapped-ion) and which near-term device strategies (used in recent QAE demonstrations) most naturally combine with BIQAE?
What is the optimal choice of per-stage sample sizes and incremental batch sizes in practice, and how sensitive is algorithmic performance to those choices?
How would BIQAE interact with alternative QAE variants (e.g., BAE, RAE) if one mixes Bayesian experiment design and Bayesian posterior maintenance—can hybrid schemes yield further gains?
What is the tradeoff between classical overhead (sampling + fitting priors in Beta-BIQAE) and quantum shot savings in latency- or throughput-constrained environments?

Developing Bayesian-informed schedules (similar in spirit to BAE) to further exploit limited measurement information and potentially improve constant factors in sample complexity.

Combining BIQAE with NISQ accommodations and strategies from existing experimental QAE demonstrations (e.g., noise tailoring, robust amplitude estimation techniques) to facilitate practical hardware implementation.

Demonstrating BIQAE on real quantum hardware when sufficiently reliable logical qubits and low-error gates are available (far-term demonstration), and exploring near-term demonstrations with appropriate noise mitigation.
Exploring further schemes and new approaches to capitalize on Bayesian inference across QAE and more broadly to reduce measurement cost in quantum algorithms.
Investigating leveraging Bayesian optimization or other Bayesian experimental-design tools to optimize BIQAE schedules and hyperparameters automatically.
key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — BIQAE (Bayesian Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation) demonstrates analytically and empirically a consistent double-digit percentage reduction in quantum sample complexity versus IQAE and several QAE variants in simulated experiments.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The algorithm integrates classical Bayesian inference (posterior updates, credible intervals, MLE-based prior fitting) with iterative quantum amplitude amplification, forming a hybrid quantum-classical pipeline per stage.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — By building on iterative QAE (IQAE) and using VQE for state preparation, BIQAE targets a more NISQ-friendly regime than QFT-based QAE, using small per-stage shot batches (Nincre=10) and adaptive stage sizes.

#idea:quantum-advantage — The authors derive asymptotic mean-squared-error (AMSE) and sample-complexity bounds under normal approximations that attribute reductions to Bayesian updates, giving theoretical support to empirical gains.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Two concrete implementations (Normal-BIQAE with CLT/normal approximations and Beta-BIQAE with exact binomial conjugacy and MLE-based prior fitting) show trade-offs and both yield improved credible-interval radii and median absolute error in simulations.

#idea:hybrid-approach — BIQAE includes practical algorithmic components: BayesianUpdate, ComputeCRI (credible intervals mapped to theta via nonlinear fk), FindNextK linear-search schedule selection (base-3 and base-3/base-5 schedules), and PreparePrior for nonlinear prior propagation.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Empirical validation comprises extensive synthetic amplitude-scaling studies (mock Q operators emulated by RY rotations) and molecular ground-state energy estimation (H2, LiH, HF, BeH2) prepared by VQE, showing reductions in weighted shots and improvements in coverage and error metrics.

#limitation:simulation-only — All experiments were classical numerical simulations (mock Q operators and zero-shot Pauli expectation computation); no physical QPU experiments were performed to validate performance on real hardware.
#limitation:noise — Results are obtained under ideal (noiseless) simulation assumptions; the impact of device noise, decoherence, and error mitigation on BIQAE performance is not evaluated.

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — Despite robust statistical repetition (200–1000 runs) and benchmarking against many QAE variants, the absence of hardware runs leaves open whether observed sample-complexity gains translate to noisy devices or production workflows.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Demonstrations on small molecular problems using qubit tapering (effective qubit counts down to ~6–7) indicate applicability to small chemistry instances; transfer to large-scale finance Monte Carlo problems is plausible but not demonstrated.

#idea:quantum-advantage — The paper's methodological contributions (Bayesian schedule design and prior propagation techniques) are broadly transferable to other QAE applications (e.g., quantum Monte Carlo in finance), though such cross-domain experiments are not included.
